lead: A DFA is easy to draw as a picture and easy to write as a table. The picture is a transition diagram: circles for states, an arrow into the start state, double circles for final states, and labelled edges for moves. The table has one row per state and one column per symbol. To talk about a whole string, not just one symbol, we extend the transition function to δ̂. It answers the question 'where do I finish after reading this string?' and gives the formal definition of the language accepted by the machine. Compilers, hardware controllers and text search use the same table.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for strings and languages, and 1.2 for the DFA model.

blocks.text: A transition diagram is a directed graph. Each state is a circle. The start state q₀ has a short incoming arrow with no source. Each final state has a double circle. For each state q and symbol a, a directed edge goes from q to δ(q, a) and is labelled a. If two symbols cause the same move, draw two parallel edges, one per symbol. Some books combine them as one edge with labels separated by commas; both mean the same.

A transition table gives the same facts in rows. One row per state, one column per symbol. The entry in row q and column a is the state δ(q, a). Mark the start state with → and each final state with *. A DFA table has exactly one entry in every cell.
The diagram is for people; the table is for machines and for checking every case. The two must agree on every entry.

δ reads one symbol. A string contains many symbols. Define δ̂ (some books write δ*) from states × Σ* to states. It says: δ̂(q, ε) = q, and δ̂(q, wa) = δ(δ̂(q, w), a). Here q is a state, w is a string, a is a symbol, ε is the empty string, and δ is the one-step transition function.
δ̂(q, ε) = q;   δ̂(q, wa) = δ(δ̂(q, w), a)
blocks.where: q is a state; w is a string; a is a symbol; ε is the empty string; δ is the one-step transition function.

blocks.text: The second equation peels the last symbol a. To process wa, first process the prefix w, then take one more step on a. Reading a string a₁a₂...aₙ from left to right gives δ(...δ(δ(q, a₁), a₂)..., aₙ).
The language accepted by M is L(M) = { w ∈ Σ* : δ̂(q₀, w) ∈ F }.
L(M) = { w ∈ Σ* : δ̂(q₀, w) ∈ F }
blocks.where: Σ is the alphabet; q₀ is the start state; F is the set of final states; δ̂ is the extended transition function.

items: Claim: δ̂(q, xy) = δ̂(δ̂(q, x), y) for all strings x and y.
Base: |y| = 0, so y = ε. δ̂(q, xε) = δ̂(q, x) = δ̂(δ̂(q, x), ε).
Step: assume the claim for y. Then δ̂(q, x(ya)) = δ̂(q, (xy)a) = δ(δ̂(q, xy), a) = δ(δ̂(δ̂(q, x), y), a) = δ̂(δ̂(q, x), ya).

sections.h3: Tracing a string column by column

blocks.text: To compute δ̂(q₀, w), write the current state above each prefix of w. Start with q₀ for prefix ε. For each new symbol a, look up the row of the current state and the column a. Move to that entry. After the last symbol, the current state is δ̂(q₀, w). Accept exactly when this state is in F.
The figure shows δ̂(A, 1001). The rows are prefixes, not separate runs. The last row gives C, a final state, so 1001 is accepted.
For 110: A on ε, A on 1, A on 11, then B on 110. B is not final, so 110 is rejected. This is the whole decision procedure for a DFA: one pass, left to right, no backtracking.

figure.caption: Each column is one more symbol read and the state reached after it. For 1001 the run ends in C, a final state, so it is accepted; for 110 it ends in B and is rejected.

examples.question: For the DFA with states A, B, C, start state A, final state C, and transitions δ(A,0)=B, δ(A,1)=A, δ(B,0)=B, δ(B,1)=C, δ(C,0)=C, δ(C,1)=C, compute δ̂(A, 1001) and δ̂(A, 110). Decide whether each string is accepted.
steps: δ̂(A, 1001) = δ(B, 1) = C. C is final, so 1001 is accepted.
For 110: δ̂(A, ε)=A; δ̂(A, 1)=δ(A, 1)=A; δ̂(A, 11)=δ(A, 1)=A; δ̂(A, 110)=δ(A, 0)=B. B is not final, so 110 is rejected.
examples.answer: δ̂(A, 1001)=C and 1001 is accepted; δ̂(A, 110)=B and 110 is rejected. Numbering A=0, B=1, C=2 and writing acceptance as 1 or 0, the check prints 2, 1, 1, 0.

traps: δ takes one symbol; δ̂ takes a whole string. Never write δ(q, w) for a string w.
The definition δ̂(q, wa) = δ(δ̂(q, w), a) peels the last symbol in the equation, but the computation still reads the string from left to right.
In a DFA transition table every entry is exactly one state. A set of states appears only for an NFA, in the next chapter.
Two parallel edges labelled with different symbols and one edge labelled with both symbols mean the same machine. Use the drawing style your exam follows.

quiz.q: What does a double circle mean in a transition diagram?
Write the two equations that define δ̂(q, w).
quiz.a: δ̂(q, ε) = q and δ̂(q, wa) = δ(δ̂(q, w), a).

quiz.q: Why does the definition of δ̂ use δ on the right-hand side?
quiz.a: A string is built from symbols. To process wa, first process the prefix w to reach a state, then apply the one-symbol transition δ on a.

quiz.q: In a transition table, what is the entry in row q and column a?
quiz.a: The state δ(q, a), the unique state the DFA moves to from q on symbol a.

quiz.q: For the DFA in the worked example, compute δ̂(A, 101).
quiz.a: δ̂(A,1)=A, δ̂(A,10)=B, δ̂(A,101)=C. The state is C.

quiz.q: For the same DFA, trace δ̂(A, 0101) and decide acceptance.
quiz.a: A on ε; read 0 → B; read 1 → C; read 0 → C; read 1 → C. δ̂(A,0101)=C, which is final, so 0101 is accepted.

quiz.q: Prove δ̂(q, xy) = δ̂(δ̂(q, x), y) by induction on |y|.
quiz.a: Base y=ε: δ̂(q,xε)=δ̂(q,x)=δ̂(δ̂(q,x),ε). Step: assume for y; δ̂(q,x(ya))=δ̂(q,(xy)a)=δ(δ̂(q,xy),a)=δ(δ̂(δ̂(q,x),y),a)=δ̂(δ̂(q,x),ya).

beyond: Not for the exam. Transition tables are the input format for lexer generators and regular-expression engines. Hardware controllers and network protocols are often specified as state diagrams. Tools that draw automata from a table are common in teaching and in formal verification. Search next for 'DFA transition table', 'automata visualizer' and 'lexical analyzer DFA'.
